items.name: Disposable nitrile gloves
items.need: Gloves keep waste, sewage and bleach off your skin at a time when you cannot wash your hands properly afterwards.
items.how_to_choose: Buy powder-free nitrile, not latex, so allergies are not a problem. Thin exam gloves (about 3 to 4 mil) are fine for quick jobs. For tying off toilet bags, scrubbing or handling bleach, 6 mil or more tears far less often. A box of 100 is about the size of a tissue box, so storage is not an issue. Check your hand size before you buy; a glove that is too small rips when you pull it on.

qty.note: One box of 100 gloves (50 pairs) per household for two weeks. That allows three to four pairs a day for toilet-bag changes and cleaning. Add a second box for five or more people, or if someone is ill. This is this site's estimate, not an official figure.

items.already_own: Any unopened box of powder-free nitrile or vinyl gloves will do. Pull one on and stretch it: if it tears easily, feels sticky or has gone brittle, replace the box. Reusable dish gloves also work for cleaning if you disinfect them after each use and keep them only for that job.

safety_notes.text: Wear rubber or disposable gloves when you clean up vomit or diarrhea and when you handle soiled laundry. Wash your hands afterwards.
Gloves do not replace handwashing. Wash with soap and water after you take them off, even if they did not tear.
Wear gloves when using bleach if the label says to, and wash your hands after cleaning or disinfecting.

items.name: Alcohol hand sanitizer
items.need: When the taps are dry, sanitizer is the fallback for cleaning your hands after the toilet and before eating.
items.how_to_choose: Check the label for at least 60% alcohol. Buy a known brand from a regular store, not an unfamiliar name from a marketplace. A pump bottle that can sit by the toilet and the food area gets used more than a pocket bottle. Sanitizer is a backup: keep some water and soap for hands that are visibly dirty or after caring for someone with vomiting or diarrhea.

qty.note: One 12 fl oz bottle for each person aged 6 or over, and never fewer than one for the household; one bottle covers 3 days or two weeks. An adult cleans a younger child's hands, and the bottle stays out of a small child's reach. Arithmetic: about 8 uses a day at roughly 0.1 fl oz (3 mL) each is about 0.8 fl oz a day, or about 11.4 fl oz in 14 days; the bottle holds 12 fl oz. The amount per use and 8 uses a day are this site's assumptions; CDC only says to cover all surfaces of both hands.
qty.rule: 1 for each person aged 6 or over, and never fewer than 1 for the household. An adult cleans a younger child's hands, and the bottle stays out of a small child's reach

items.already_own: Any sanitizer you already have is fine if the label shows 60% alcohol or more, it is within its expiry date, and its maker is not on the FDA's do-not-use list. Check how much is left against the per-person amount above.

safety_notes.text: Washing with soap and water is the best way to clean hands in most situations. Use sanitizer only when soap and water are not available.
Use a sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol. Cover all surfaces of both hands and rub until dry, which takes about 20 seconds. Do not wipe it off early.
Sanitizer does not kill all germs and may not work well on visibly dirty or greasy hands. Soap and water work better against norovirus, Cryptosporidium and C. difficile.
Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus. It can be used in addition to handwashing but not instead of it.

Hand sanitizer is flammable, and drinking even a small amount can cause alcohol poisoning in a child. Store it away from heat and flame and out of reach of children and pets, supervise children who use it, and let hands dry fully before going near a flame.
safety_notes.research_note: Re-opened 2026-11-16 (FDA, Safely Using Hand Sanitizer, content current as of 04/12/2023): supervise children using hand sanitizer; store out of reach of pets and children; drinking even a small amount can cause alcohol poisoning in children; flammable, keep away from heat and flames, rub until fully dry.

item_flags: Reasons products are on the FDA list include methanol, 1-propanol, benzene, acetaldehyde and acetal contamination, too little alcohol, microbial contamination, packaging that looks like a drink or food pouch, and makers that did not answer FDA records requests. Avoid unfamiliar brands and anything packaged like a drink.

items.name: Rinse-free bathing wipes
items.need: With no running water, large bathing wipes let each person wash their whole body every day and avoid rashes and infections.
items.how_to_choose: For a full-body wash, adult bathing wipes are bigger and thicker than baby wipes. Look at the cost per wash, not the pack price. A single large wipe per wash is the cheapest route; an eight-cloth pack gives a fuller wash, one cloth per body area. Sealed or individually wrapped packs do not dry out in a closet. Used wipes go in the trash, never down the toilet.

qty.note: An optional extra: it has no baseline quantity and stays out of the totals. Baby wipes are fine for hands and face: one pack of 60 to 80 per person per week (U5-01). If you also want a full wash, plan one per person per day; each pick's size line shows how many washes one pack gives.

items.already_own: Baby wipes or facial wipes you already have will do for a few days if you use several per wash. Check that the pack is still moist and has not passed its date. A washcloth with a cup of water and a little soap also works if you can spare the water.

safety_notes.text: Never flush wipes of any kind. Flush only toilet paper; wipes can block the pipes in your building and the sewers beyond it. Put used wipes in the trash.
safety_notes.source_title: EPA Encourages Americans to Only Flush Toilet Paper

safety_notes.text: A body wipe does not count as hand hygiene. After using the toilet or handling waste, wash with soap and water, or use a sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol if there is none.

items.name: Low-water handwashing station
items.need: A jug with a tap over a basin lets you wash your hands properly with soap using a cup of water or less each time.
items.how_to_choose: You need three things: a container with a spigot you can open and close easily, soap, and a basin or bucket underneath to catch the dirty water. Keep it small. A 2.5 to 3 gallon jug weighs about 25 lb full, fits on a counter and can be refilled from your stored water. A slow, steady flow saves water, and a tap you can shut with a wrist or elbow keeps clean hands clean. Empty the basin into the tub or a working drain, never onto a balcony.

qty.note: One station per household, set up next to the toilet area or the kitchen. Add a bar or bottle of soap and a basin or bucket to catch the water.

items.already_own: A drinks cooler or water dispenser with a spigot, set on the edge of a counter over a bucket, does the same job. Check that the tap does not drip when closed and that you can work it with soapy hands.

safety_notes.text: Wash hands with soap and clean water poured or run over them, never in a tub or basin of water that has already been used. CDC says hands can pick up germs from water that looks dirty, is contaminated or has been used before, which is why it recommends clean, running water. So hands are never washed in the dish tubs.
If clean tap water is not available, CDC says to make a temporary handwashing station from a large water jug.
safety_notes.source_title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Wet your hands with clean water, lather with soap, scrub for at least 20 seconds including the backs of the hands, between the fingers and under the nails, rinse, and dry with a clean towel.
Wash after using the toilet, before preparing food or eating, after touching trash, and before and after caring for someone who is sick with vomiting or diarrhea.
Soap and water is the best way to clean hands in most situations and works better than sanitizer against norovirus, Cryptosporidium and C. difficile, and on dirty hands.

budget.size: 2.6 US gal (10 L); 8 x 8 x 2.5 in and 6 oz as GSI lists it; built-in tap. Also sold in 4-gallon (15 L) and 5.3-gallon (20 L) sizes.
budget.why: A do-it-yourself station: set the cube on a counter edge with the spigot over a bucket or dishpan, and add soap. Outdoor Life named it the best collapsible container, with good flow from the spigot and no separate air vent to fiddle with, and it folds flat when the emergency is over.

items.name: Hand-powered laundry
items.need: Over two to four weeks without power or running water, you need a way to wash underwear, socks and soiled items in a gallon or so of water.
items.how_to_choose: In an apartment, small and foldable beats big. A wash bag does a couple of shirts or a few pairs of underwear at a time, uses little water and stores in a drawer. Plan how you will dry things: wring hard, then hang over the tub. Wash little and often, and keep heavy items such as jeans and towels for when services return.

qty.note: One per household. Add laundry detergent and a line or rack for drying over the tub.

items.already_own: A clean bucket or the bathtub, a little detergent and your gloved hands work. Agitate for a few minutes, soak, rinse once and wring hard. A new, unused sink plunger kept only for laundry makes the agitation easier.

safety_notes.text: Handle clothes or bedding soiled with vomit or diarrhea carefully and without shaking them, wear rubber or disposable gloves, and wash your hands afterwards. CDC's advice is a hot machine wash on the longest cycle and a hot dryer, which hand washing cannot match, so bag badly soiled items until a machine is available if you can.

Rinse off visible stool before washing, use the hottest water that is safe for the fabric, add chlorine bleach if the item can take it, and wash your hands after handling laundry even if you wore gloves.

items.name: Surface disinfectant
items.need: After vomiting, diarrhea or contact with sewage, surfaces need a disinfectant that is proven to kill gut germs such as norovirus.
items.how_to_choose: Look for an EPA registration number on the label and check it against EPA's List G, the products shown to kill norovirus. Bleach-based products are on that list; the common bleach-free household wipes are not. Plain disinfecting bleach is the cheapest and strongest but must be mixed fresh each day. A ready-to-use bleach spray needs no mixing, which helps when water is short. Store bleach products low down, away from ammonia and other cleaners.

qty.note: One bottle or canister per household, plus paper towels or rags you can throw away.

items.already_own: A bottle of regular, unscented household bleach works if the label shows 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite and it is not splashless or laundry-only bleach. For any other cleaner, find the EPA Reg. No. on the label and look it up on EPA's List G before relying on it for illness or sewage clean-up.

safety_notes.text: To disinfect a surface with bleach, clean it with soap or detergent first, then follow the surface-disinfecting directions on your own bottle's label. Only if the label gives none, CDC's mix for regular unscented bleach (5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite) is 5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) per gallon of room-temperature water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Keep the surface wet for at least 1 minute.

After vomiting or diarrhea, CDC's surface mix is stronger: 5 to 25 tablespoons of household bleach (5% to 8%) per gallon of water, which gives 1,000 to 5,000 ppm chlorine. Leave it on for at least 5 minutes, then clean the area again with soap and hot water. Wear rubber or disposable gloves.

The mixes above are for surfaces only and must never be used on water you will drink. Making water safe to drink is a different job with its own, far smaller dose: CDC says to follow the drinking-water instructions on the bleach label, and gives a table counted in drops only for a label that has none. That table is with the water bleach item on this site, not here.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Never mix bleach, or any disinfectant, with ammonia or any other cleaner; the mix can release dangerous gases. Open windows and doors while you work.
Mix a fresh bleach solution every day. A diluted solution loses strength after about 24 hours.

EPA's List G names the registered disinfectants that EPA has confirmed kill norovirus, and List K names those that kill C. difficile spores. Match the EPA Reg. No. on your bottle to the list and follow the label's contact time.
safety_notes.source_title: EPA's Registered Antimicrobial Products Effective Against Norovirus (feline calicivirus) [List G]

safety_notes.text: Never flush disinfecting wipes. Put them in the trash.
safety_notes.source_title: EPA Encourages Americans to Only Flush Toilet Paper

item_flags: Ordinary Clorox Disinfecting Wipes (EPA Reg. No. 5813-79) are bleach-free and are not on EPA's List G for norovirus. Do not rely on them after vomiting, diarrhea or sewage contact.
CDC says not to use splashless or laundry-only bleach, or bleach with no stated strength, for disinfecting.

items.name: Menstrual supplies
items.need: A period does not wait for the water to come back, so anyone who menstruates needs a supply that works with little or no washing water.
items.how_to_choose: This applies only to people who menstruate. Boxed disposable pads are the simplest backup: they store for years, need no water and nothing is inserted with hands you could not wash. A menstrual cup takes almost no space and lasts for years, but it needs clean hands and a little clean water to rinse, and should be boiled between cycles. Period underwear must be rinsed and washed, so it costs the most water. Keep pads on hand even if you normally use a cup.

qty.note: One supply for each person at home who menstruates, teenagers included; not one per household and not one per adult. The site does not ask who menstruates, so count for yourself. One supply is one full cycle of what that person uses, beyond what is open now, and two cycles at a two-week or longer target. For pads, one pack of 32 or more per cycle is this site's estimate.

items.already_own: Use whatever you normally use and simply keep one extra cycle's worth in the closet. Check that pad and tampon wrappers are intact and dry. If you rely on a cup or period underwear, add a box of disposable pads for days when you cannot wash.

safety_notes.text: If you use tampons, change them every 4 to 8 hours and never leave one in for more than 8 hours, use the lowest absorbency you need, and wash your hands before and after. Toxic shock syndrome is rare but serious: stop use and get medical help for sudden fever, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness or a sunburn-like rash.
safety_notes.source_title: The Facts on Tampons and Tampon Safety

safety_notes.text: FDA has not authorized any reusable tampon and discourages their use because of added infection risk.
safety_notes.source_title: The Facts on Tampons and Tampon Safety

safety_notes.text: Clean your hands before and after changing any menstrual product. Use soap and water, or a sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol when there is no water.
Do not flush pads, tampons, liners or wipes. Flush only toilet paper; wrap used products and put them in the trash.
safety_notes.source_title: EPA Encourages Americans to Only Flush Toilet Paper
